claims.source: Bedaquiline binds the membrane region of mycobacterial ATP synthase (Andries et al., 2005; Guo et al., 2021; Preiss et al., 2015), blocking proton translocation and ATP synthesis.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Andries et al., 2005; Guo et al., 2021; Preiss et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Bedaquiline established oxidative phosphorylation as a target space for antibiotics against mycobacteria.
claims.source: Thus, in addition to providing an invaluable therapeutic tool, bedaquiline established oxidative phosphorylation as a target space for antibiotics against mycobacteria.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the success of bedaquiline as a therapeutic.

claims.claim: Numerous compounds have been identified that target either ATP synthase or the electron transport chain complexes that establish the transmembrane proton motive force.
claims.source: Subsequent to the discovery of bedaquiline, numerous compounds have been identified that target either ATP synthase or the electron transport chain complexes that establish the transmembrane proton motive force (PMF) that drives ATP synthesis (Cook et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Cook et al., 2017.

claims.claim: In mammalian mitochondrial electron transport chains, complexes I and II oxidize NADH and succinate, respectively.
claims.source: In mammalian mitochondrial electron transport chains, complexes I and II oxidize NADH (the reduced form of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide) and succinate, respectively.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about mammalian electron transport chains.

claims.claim: Electrons from NADH and succinate are used to reduce a membrane-bound pool of ubiquinone to ubiquinol in mammalian mitochondria.
claims.source: The electrons from these substrates are used to reduce a membrane-bound pool of ubiquinone (UQ) to ubiquinol (UQH2).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about mammalian electron transport chains.

claims.claim: Electrons from ubiquinol are passed successively to CIII, soluble cyt. c, and CIV before ultimately reducing molecular oxygen to water in mammalian mitochondria.
claims.source: Electrons from UQH2 are then passed successively to CIII (also known as cytochrome [cyt.] bc1), soluble cyt. c, and CIV (also known as cyt. c oxidase or cyt. aa3) before ultimately reducing molecular oxygen to water.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about mammalian electron transport chains.

claims.claim: Complexes I, III, and IV couple electron transfer to proton transfer across the membrane in mammalian mitochondria.
claims.source: Complexes I, III, and IV couple electron transfer to proton transfer across the membrane, thereby generating the PMF that drives ATP synthesis.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about mammalian electron transport chains.

claims.claim: Mycobacteria possess a branched electron transport chain.
claims.source: In contrast to mitochondria and many bacteria, mycobacteria possess a branched electron transport chain (reviewed in Cook et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Cook et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Mycobacterial respiration relies on menaquinone as an intermediate electron carrier rather than ubiquinone.
claims.source: Rather than UQ, mycobacterial respiration relies on menaquinone (MQ) as an intermediate electron carrier.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about mycobacterial electron transport chains, supported by citation to Cook et al., 2017.

claims.claim: MQH2 can reduce molecular oxygen via two MQH2:O2 oxidoreductases in mycobacteria: cyt. bd and cyt. bcc-aa3.
claims.source: MQH2 can reduce molecular oxygen via two MQH2:O2 oxidoreductases: cyt. bd and cyt. bcc-aa3, the latter being equivalent to a combination of canonical CIII and CIV with the stoichiometry CIII2CIV2.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about mycobacterial electron transport chains.

claims.claim: CIII2CIV2 transfers three protons across the membrane for each electron used to reduce O2.
claims.source: The CIII2CIV2 supercomplex and cyt. bd branches of the mycobacterial electron transport chain are bioenergetically not equivalent, while CIII2CIV2 transfers three protons across the membrane for each electron used to reduce O2, cyt. bd transfers the equivalent of only one proton across the membrane for each electron.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about the bioenergetics of mycobacterial electron transport chains.

claims.claim: Cyt. bd transfers the equivalent of only one proton across the membrane for each electron used to reduce O2.
claims.source: The CIII2CIV2 supercomplex and cyt. bd branches of the mycobacterial electron transport chain are bioenergetically not equivalent, while CIII2CIV2 transfers three protons across the membrane for each electron used to reduce O2, cyt. bd transfers the equivalent of only one proton across the membrane for each electron.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about the bioenergetics of mycobacterial electron transport chains.

claims.claim: Enzyme utilization in mycobacterial electron transport chains can adapt to changes in environmental conditions and treatment with respiratory complex inhibitors.
claims.source: Enzyme utilization in mycobacterial electron transport chains can adapt to changes in environmental conditions and treatment with respiratory complex inhibitors (Arora et al., 2014; Berney and Cook, 2010), which complicates targeting of respiration by antimycobacterial drugs (Beites et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Arora et al., 2014; Berney and Cook, 2010; Beites et al., 2019.

claims.claim: A dimeric type C superoxide dismutase (SOD) is an integral component of the CIII2CIV2 supercomplex from M. smegmatis.
claims.source: Structural analysis of the CIII2CIV2 supercomplex from M. smegmatis led to the discovery that a dimeric type C superoxide dismutase (SOD) is an integral component of the assembly (Gong et al., 2018; Wiseman et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gong et al., 2018; Wiseman et al., 2018.

claims.claim: The SOD dimer is found on the periplasmic side of CIII2CIV2.
claims.source: The SOD dimer is found on the periplasmic side of CIII2CIV2 and is held in place by its two N-terminal tails, which bind to the complex's QcrA subunits.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gong et al., 2018; Wiseman et al., 2018.

claims.claim: The SOD dimer is held in place by its two N-terminal tails, which bind to the complex's QcrA subunits.
claims.source: The SOD dimer is found on the periplasmic side of CIII2CIV2 and is held in place by its two N-terminal tails, which bind to the complex's QcrA subunits.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gong et al., 2018; Wiseman et al., 2018.

claims.claim: QcrA has 81.4% sequence similarity and 73.2% sequence identity between M. smegmatis and M. tuberculosis.
claims.source: Both QcrA and the SOD subunits are highly conserved between M. smegmatis and M. tuberculosis, with 81.4% and 71.0% sequence similarity and 73.2% and 64.8% sequence identity, respectively, suggesting that a similar association occurs in the M. tuberculosis enzyme.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on sequence comparison data.

claims.claim: SOD subunits have 71.0% sequence similarity and 64.8% sequence identity between M. smegmatis and M. tuberculosis.
claims.source: Both QcrA and the SOD subunits are highly conserved between M. smegmatis and M. tuberculosis, with 81.4% and 71.0% sequence similarity and 73.2% and 64.8% sequence identity, respectively, suggesting that a similar association occurs in the M. tuberculosis enzyme.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on sequence comparison data.

claims.claim: A similar SOD association likely occurs in the M. tuberculosis CIII2CIV2 enzyme.
claims.source: Both QcrA and the SOD subunits are highly conserved between M. smegmatis and M. tuberculosis, with 81.4% and 71.0% sequence similarity and 73.2% and 64.8% sequence identity, respectively, suggesting that a similar association occurs in the M. tuberculosis enzyme.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on sequence conservation data.

claims.claim: M. tuberculosis mutants that lack SOD are susceptible to killing within macrophages.
claims.source: M. tuberculosis mutants that lack SOD are susceptible to killing within macrophages (Piddington et al., 2001), emphasizing the importance of the subunit.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Piddington et al., 2001.

claims.claim: The SOD subunit may abstract electrons from reactive oxygen species formed during respiration or generated by host-defense mechanisms and direct them through the respiratory chain to contribute to the PMF and ATP synthesis.
claims.source: Given its position within CIII2CIV2, it is possible that the SOD subunit abstracts electrons from reactive oxygen species formed during respiration or generated by host-defense mechanisms in the phagolysosome upon phagocytosis of M. tuberculosis and directs them through the respiratory chain to contribute to the PMF and ATP synthesis (Gong et al., 2018; Wiseman et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the position of SOD within CIII2CIV2.

claims.claim: Killing of M. tuberculosis with electron transport chain inhibitors may require simultaneously blocking both the CIII2CIV2 and cyt. bd branches for oxygen reduction.
claims.source: Although killing of M. tuberculosis with electron transport chain inhibitors may require simultaneously blocking both the CIII2CIV2 and cyt. bd branches for oxygen reduction (Arora et al., 2014; Beites et al., 2019; Matsoso et al., 2005), high-profile candidate TB therapeutics have been identified that bind to CIII within CIII2CIV2 (Pethe et al., 2013; Rybniker et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Arora et al., 2014; Beites et al., 2019; Matsoso et al., 2005.

claims.claim: High-profile candidate TB therapeutics have been identified that bind to CIII within CIII2CIV2.
claims.source: Although killing of M. tuberculosis with electron transport chain inhibitors may require simultaneously blocking both the CIII2CIV2 and cyt. bd branches for oxygen reduction (Arora et al., 2014; Beites et al., 2019; Matsoso et al., 2005), high-profile candidate TB therapeutics have been identified that bind to CIII within CIII2CIV2 (Pethe et al., 2013; Rybniker et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Pethe et al., 2013; Rybniker et al., 2015.

claims.claim: CIII2CIV2 is not essential in M. smegmatis.
claims.source: Similarly, while CIII2CIV2 is not essential in M. smegmatis, its disruption causes severe growth defects (Matsoso et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Matsoso et al., 2005.

claims.claim: Disruption of CIII2CIV2 causes severe growth defects in M. smegmatis.
claims.source: Similarly, while CIII2CIV2 is not essential in M. smegmatis, its disruption causes severe growth defects (Matsoso et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Matsoso et al., 2005.

claims.claim: CIII2CIV2 is essential in M. leprae and M. ulcerans.
claims.source: In contrast, CIII2CIV2 is essential in M. leprae and M. ulcerans, which lack the cyt. bd branch of the electron transport chain entirely (Cole et al., 2001; Demangel et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cole et al., 2001; Demangel et al., 2009.

claims.claim: M. leprae and M. ulcerans lack the cyt. bd branch of the electron transport chain entirely.
claims.source: In contrast, CIII2CIV2 is essential in M. leprae and M. ulcerans, which lack the cyt. bd branch of the electron transport chain entirely (Cole et al., 2001; Demangel et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cole et al., 2001; Demangel et al., 2009.

claims.claim: CIII contributes to the PMF by separating positive and negative charges across the membrane through a mechanism known as the Q cycle.
claims.source: Rather than pumping protons, CIII contributes to the PMF by separating positive and negative charges across the membrane through a mechanism known as the Q cycle (reviewed in Sarewicz and Osyczka, 2015; Xia et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about CIII function, supported by citations to Sarewicz and Osyczka, 2015; Xia et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Each CIII contains two sites where redox reactions with MQ occur: a QP site near the positive side of the membrane and a QN site near the negative side of the membrane.
claims.source: Each CIII contains two sites where redox reactions with MQ occur: a QP site near the positive (periplasmic) side of the membrane where MQH2 is oxidized and a QN site near the negative (cytoplasmic) side of the membrane where MQ is reduced.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about CIII structure and function.

claims.claim: Oxidation of MQH2 in the QP site leads to release of two protons to the positive side of the membrane.
claims.source: In the current understanding of the Q cycle in mycobacteria, oxidation of MQH2 in the QP site leads to release of two protons to the positive side of the membrane.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about the Q cycle mechanism.

claims.claim: The first electron from MQH2 oxidation is passed to a [2Fe–2S] Rieske center in subunit QcrA where it consecutively reduces the cyt. cc domain of the QcrC subunit and the CuA di-nuclear center of CIV.
claims.source: The first electron from this oxidation reaction is passed to a [2Fe–2S] Rieske center (FeS) in subunit QcrA where it consecutively reduces the cyt. cc domain of the QcrC subunit and the CuA di-nuclear center of CIV.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about the Q cycle mechanism.

claims.claim: The second electron from MQH2 in the QP site is transferred first to heme bL and then heme bH before reducing a MQ molecule in the QN site to MQ•-.
claims.source: The second electron from the MQH2 in the QP site is transferred first to heme bL and then heme bH, both in subunit QcrB of CIII, before reducing a MQ molecule in the QN site to MQ•-.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about the Q cycle mechanism.

claims.claim: Within CIV, electrons are transferred from the CuA di-nuclear center to O2 bound at the heme a3-CuB binuclear catalytic site via heme a, driving proton pumping across the membrane.
claims.source: Within CIV, electrons are transferred from the CuA di-nuclear center to O2 bound at the heme a3-CuB binuclear catalytic site via heme a, driving proton pumping across the membrane.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about CIV function.

claims.claim: Telacebec was identified in a screen of macrophages infected with M. tuberculosis.
claims.source: Telacebec (also known as Q203) was identified in a screen of macrophages infected with M. tuberculosis (Pethe et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Pethe et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Generation of resistance mutants bearing T313I and T313A mutations in the qcrB gene indicated that telacebec targets CIII of the CIII2CIV2 supercomplex.
claims.source: Generation of resistance mutants bearing T313I and T313A mutations in the qcrB gene indicated that telacebec targets CIII of the CIII2CIV2 supercomplex.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on resistance mutation data, supported by citation to Pethe et al., 2013.

claims.claim: A recent Phase 2 clinical trial demonstrated a decrease in viable mycobacterial sputum load with increasing dose of telacebec.
claims.source: A recent Phase 2 clinical trial demonstrated a decrease in viable mycobacterial sputum load with increasing dose of telacebec, supporting further development and making telacebec one of only a few new drug classes in more than 50 years with demonstrated antituberculosis activity in humans (de Jager et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to de Jager et al., 2020.

claims.claim: Telacebec may have clinical utility in treating nontuberculosis mycobacterial infections, such as Buruli ulcer.
claims.source: Telacebec may also have clinical utility in treating nontuberculosis mycobacterial infections, such as Buruli ulcer (Almeida et al., 2020; Van Der Werf et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative claim supported by citations to Almeida et al., 2020; Van Der Werf et al., 2020.

claims.claim: The M. tuberculosis telacebec resistance mutations T313A and T313I are equivalent to mutation of Thr308 in M. smegmatis.
claims.source: The M. tuberculosis telacebec resistance mutations T313A and T313I (Pethe et al., 2013), equivalent to mutation of Thr308 in M. smegmatis, are near the QP site and suggest that the inhibitor could interfere with MQH2 binding to CIII2CIV2.
claims.evidence: This is based on sequence alignment and structural analysis.

claims.claim: The telacebec resistance mutations are near the QP site and suggest that the inhibitor could interfere with MQH2 binding to CIII2CIV2.
claims.source: The M. tuberculosis telacebec resistance mutations T313A and T313I (Pethe et al., 2013), equivalent to mutation of Thr308 in M. smegmatis, are near the QP site and suggest that the inhibitor could interfere with MQH2 binding to CIII2CIV2.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the location of resistance mutations and structural data.

claims.claim: Purification of CIII2CIV2 from M. smegmatis grown in TDS-supplemented medium gave a high yield of enzyme with clear bands on an SDS-PAGE gel for most of the known subunits of the complex.
claims.source: Purification of CIII2CIV2 from M. smegmatis grown in these conditions gave a high yield of enzyme with clear bands on an SDS-PAGE gelfor most of the known subunits of the complex (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: Gel filtration chromatography of CIII2CIV2 led to depletion of the LpqE and SOD subunits.
claims.source: We observed that following affinity purification, gel filtration chromatography of the enzyme led to depletion of the LpqE and SOD subunits (Figure 1A, right) compared to affinity purification alone (Figure 1A, left), and consequently this purification step was avoided.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: CryoEM of the CIII2CIV2 preparation allowed for calculation of a 3D map of the enzyme at a nominal resolution of 3.0 Å.
claims.source: CryoEM of the CIII2CIV2 preparation allowed for calculation of a 3D map of the enzyme at a nominal resolution of 3.0 Å (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and Table 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and Table 1.

claims.claim: The cryoEM map shows strong density for the LpqE subunit.
claims.source: The map shows strong density for the LpqE subunit (Figure 1B, orange).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: LpqE was observed in one previous structural study of CIII2CIV2 from M. smegmatis but was absent in another.
claims.source: LpqE was observed in one previous structural study of CIII2CIV2 from M. smegmatis (Gong et al., 2018) but was absent in another (Wiseman et al., 2018), presumably due to depletion of the subunit during purification of the supercomplex.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gong et al., 2018 and Wiseman et al., 2018.

claims.claim: In the structure missing LpqE, the cyt. cc domain of subunit QcrC adopts both an 'open' and a 'closed' conformation.
claims.source: In the structure missing LpqE, the cyt. cc domain of subunit QcrC adopts both an 'open' and a 'closed' conformation, while the structure with LpqE was found only in the closed conformation.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wiseman et al., 2018.

claims.claim: The structure with LpqE was found only in the closed conformation of the cyt. cc domain.
claims.source: In the structure missing LpqE, the cyt. cc domain of subunit QcrC adopts both an 'open' and a 'closed' conformation, while the structure with LpqE was found only in the closed conformation.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gong et al., 2018.

claims.claim: The closed conformation creates a direct electronic connection between heme cII of CIII and CuA of CIV.
claims.source: The closed conformation creates a direct electronic connection between heme cII of CIII and CuA of CIV (Gong et al., 2018; Wiseman et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gong et al., 2018; Wiseman et al., 2018.

claims.claim: In the open conformation, heme cII from the cyt. cc domain is too far from CuA to allow electron transfer.
claims.source: In the open conformation, heme cII from the cyt. cc domain is too far from CuA to allow electron transfer, leading to the hypothesis that switching between the closed and open conformations plays a role in controlling the flow of electrons through the supercomplex (Wiseman et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wiseman et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Switching between the closed and open conformations of the cyt. cc domain may play a role in controlling the flow of electrons through the supercomplex.
claims.source: In the open conformation, heme cII from the cyt. cc domain is too far from CuA to allow electron transfer, leading to the hypothesis that switching between the closed and open conformations plays a role in controlling the flow of electrons through the supercomplex (Wiseman et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on structural observations, supported by citation to Wiseman et al., 2018.

claims.claim: LpqE was hypothesized to strengthen the physical attachment between CIII and CIV.
claims.source: In contrast, LpqE was hypothesized to strengthen the physical attachment between CIII and CIV (Gong et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citation to Gong et al., 2018.

claims.claim: 3DVA revealed complexes with and without LpqE.
claims.source: 3DVA with the current dataset (Punjani and Fleet, 2021), focused on one half of the supercomplex, revealed complexes with and without LpqE.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from 3DVA analysis.

claims.claim: Where LpqE was missing, the cyt. cc domain exhibits the open conformation.
claims.source: Where LpqE was missing, the cyt. cc domain exhibits the open conformation, while complexes with LpqE show only the closed conformation of cyt. cc (Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Video 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Video 1.

claims.claim: Complexes with LpqE show only the closed conformation of cyt. cc.
claims.source: Where LpqE was missing, the cyt. cc domain exhibits the open conformation, while complexes with LpqE show only the closed conformation of cyt. cc (Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Video 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Video 1.

claims.claim: Clashes between LpqE and the open conformation of cyt. cc suggest that LpqE prevents the open conformation.
claims.source: Clashes between LpqE and the open conformation of cyt. cc suggest that LpqE prevents the open conformation.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on structural analysis.

claims.claim: The SOD subunit of CIII2CIV2 was poorly resolved in previous cryoEM maps and appeared as a diffuse density.
claims.source: In previous studies, the SOD subunit of CIII2CIV2 was poorly resolved in cryoEM maps and appeared as a diffuse density (Gong et al., 2018; Wiseman et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gong et al., 2018; Wiseman et al., 2018.

claims.claim: In the present map, the overall shape of SOD was more readily apparent than in previous studies.
claims.source: In the present map, the overall shape of SOD, although still at lower density than the rest of the complex, was more readily apparent (Figure 1B, pink).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: The N-terminal anchors from the SOD dimer that bind to subunit QcrB are well resolved and terminate at the middle of the complex with a lipid anchor.
claims.source: The N-terminal anchors from the SOD dimer that bind to subunit QcrB are well resolved and terminate at the middle of the complex with a lipid anchor (Figure 1B, beige).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: 3DVA shows that SOD moves between the center of the complex to immediately above heme cI.
claims.source: 3DVA (Figure 1C, Video 2) shows that SOD moves between the center of the complex, where it was observed previously (Gong et al., 2018; Wiseman et al., 2018) to immediately above heme cI.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and Video 2.

claims.claim: The proximity of SOD to heme cI suggests that SOD may transfer electrons abstracted from superoxide in the periplasm to CIV to contribute to the PMF.
claims.source: This proximity suggests that SOD may indeed transfer electrons abstracted from superoxide in the periplasm of M. smegmatis to CIV to contribute to the PMF (Gong et al., 2018; Wiseman et al., 2018), although this hypothesis requires further testing.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on structural observations.

claims.claim: The overall resolution of the map allowed refinement of an atomic model for CIII2CIV2 including residues that could not be modeled previously.
claims.source: The overall resolution of the map, which is somewhat better than in previous studies, allowed refinement of an atomic model for CIII2CIV2 including residues T82, E83, A123 to D131, and S183 from LpqE, and residues H57 to G78 from MSMEG_4693 (also known as CtaJ), which could not be modeled previously (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 3, and Table 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 3, and Table 1.

claims.claim: The mycobacterial electron transport chain uses MQH2 as the electron donor for CIII2CIV2.
claims.source: The mycobacterial electron transport chain uses MQH2 as the electron donor for CIII2CIV2 while in canonical mitochondrial electron transport chains UQH2 donates electrons to CIII2 (Cook et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Cook et al., 2017.

claims.claim: In canonical mitochondrial electron transport chains UQH2 donates electrons to CIII2.
claims.source: The mycobacterial electron transport chain uses MQH2 as the electron donor for CIII2CIV2 while in canonical mitochondrial electron transport chains UQH2 donates electrons to CIII2 (Cook et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Cook et al., 2017.

claims.claim: The midpoint potentials of the redox centers in mycobacterial CIII2 are lower than those of canonical mitochondrial CIII2.
claims.source: The midpoint potentials of the redox centers in mycobacterial CIII2 are lower than those of canonical mitochondrial CIII2 (Kao et al., 2016), and as a result UQH2 analogues typically used in CIII2 assays are not able to reduce CIII2 of the M. smegmatis supercomplex.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kao et al., 2016.

claims.claim: UQH2 analogues typically used in CIII2 assays are not able to reduce CIII2 of the M. smegmatis supercomplex.
claims.source: The midpoint potentials of the redox centers in mycobacterial CIII2 are lower than those of canonical mitochondrial CIII2 (Kao et al., 2016), and as a result UQH2 analogues typically used in CIII2 assays are not able to reduce CIII2 of the M. smegmatis supercomplex.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the difference in midpoint potentials.

claims.claim: MQH2 analogues capable of reducing CIII2CIV2 suffer from autoxidation at neutral or basic pH.
claims.source: MQH2 analogues (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-C) capable of reducing CIII2CIV2 suffer from autoxidation at neutral or basic pH, which leads to oxygen reduction even in the absence of enzyme (Munday, 2000).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Munday, 2000.

claims.claim: Autoxidation of MQH2 analogues leads to oxygen reduction even in the absence of enzyme.
claims.source: MQH2 analogues (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-C) capable of reducing CIII2CIV2 suffer from autoxidation at neutral or basic pH, which leads to oxygen reduction even in the absence of enzyme (Munday, 2000).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Munday, 2000.

claims.claim: The rate of autoxidation was proposed to be ~30% slower for DMWH2 compared to menadiol at pH 7.5.
claims.source: Although both substrates are susceptible to autoxidation, the rate of autoxidation was proposed to be ~30% slower for DMWH2 compared to menadiol at the pH 7.5 of our oxygen consumption assays (Munday, 2000).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Munday, 2000.

claims.claim: Menaquinol autoxidized more slowly than DMWH2.
claims.source: In contrast to these earlier studies, we found that menaquinol autoxidized more slowly than DMWH2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: Menadiol was substantially less efficient than DMWH2 as an electron donor for CIII2CIV2.
claims.source: However, we also found that mendiol was substantially less efficient than DMWH2 as an electron donor for CIII2CIV2, likely due to its less favorable redox potential (Fieser and Fieser, 1934), supporting the choice of DMWH2 as the substrate in assays (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and citation to Fieser and Fieser, 1934.

claims.claim: At low concentrations of CIII2CIV2 the SOD subunit suppresses autoxidation of DMWH2 more than CIII2CIV2 catalyzes oxidation of DMWH2.
claims.source: On subsequent investigation, we realized that at low concentrations of CIII2CIV2 the SOD subunit suppresses autoxidation of DMWH2 more than CIII2CIV2 catalyzes oxidation of DMWH2.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on experimental observations.

claims.claim: Suppression of quinol autoxidation by SOD has been described previously.
claims.source: This suppression of quinol autoxidation by SOD, which has been described previously (Cadenas et al., 1988), can lead to apparent negative activities for CIII2CIV2 when the background autoxidation is subtracted.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Cadenas et al., 1988.

claims.claim: Autoxidation of quinols is believed to involve a superoxide anion intermediate.
claims.source: Autoxidation of quinols is believed to involve a superoxide anion intermediate, with the SOD-catalyzed dismutation of the intermediate to hydrogen peroxide removing this reactant to slow the process (Munday, 2000).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Munday, 2000.

claims.claim: Bovine C-type SOD can limit the autoxidation of DMWH2.
claims.source: To remove error introduced by the effect of the SOD subunit on the observed oxygen reduction signal, we established that bovine C-type SOD can similarly limit the autoxidation of DMWH2 (Figure 2A, blue and orange curves), as well as menadiol (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: With 500 nM SOD added, the CIII2CIV2's DMWH2:O2 oxidoreductase activity was measured at 91 ± 4 e-/s.
claims.source: With 500 nM SOD added, the CIII2CIV2's DMWH2:O2 oxidoreductase activity was measured at 91 ± 4 e-/s (± s.d., n = 6 independent assays with three each from two separate batches of protein), which is nearly an order of magnitude greater than the apparent activity found previously (Wiseman et al., 2018).

results.result: The authors purified CIII2CIV2 from M. smegmatis and determined its structure by cryoEM at 3.0 Å resolution, revealing improved density for the LpqE and SOD subunits and allowing modeling of previously unresolved residues.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C58, C71-C72, and C75 collectively demonstrate successful purification and structural determination of CIII2CIV2. The experimental data (SDS-PAGE, cryoEM maps, and atomic models shown in Figures 1A-D and supplementary figures) provide strong evidence for the improved resolution and identification of structural features including LpqE and SOD subunits.

results.result: 3DVA analysis revealed that LpqE presence correlates with the closed conformation of the cyt. cc domain, while LpqE absence correlates with the open conformation, suggesting that LpqE prevents the open conformation through steric clashes.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C69 are supported by 3DVA experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Video 1. The structural analysis demonstrates a clear correlation between LpqE presence/absence and cyt. cc domain conformation, with the inference about steric clashes being reasonable based on the structural data.

results.result: 3DVA shows that the SOD subunit moves between the center of the complex to immediately above heme cI, suggesting potential electron transfer from superoxide to CIV.
results.evaluation: Claim C73 is supported by experimental 3DVA data (Figure 1C, Video 2), but C74 is explicitly stated as a speculative hypothesis requiring further testing. The structural proximity alone is insufficient to demonstrate functional electron transfer without additional biochemical or biophysical validation.

results.result: The authors identified and addressed the problem of MQH2 analogue autoxidation in activity assays, finding that SOD suppresses autoxidation and that adding exogenous bovine SOD enables accurate measurement of CIII2CIV2 activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C88 describe a methodological advance supported by experimental data (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D) and citations to prior work. The observation that SOD suppresses autoxidation and the solution of adding exogenous SOD are well-documented experimentally.

results.result: With the improved assay conditions (500 nM SOD added), CIII2CIV2's DMWH2:O2 oxidoreductase activity was measured at 91 ± 4 e-/s, nearly an order of magnitude greater than previously reported.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C90 are supported by experimental activity assay data with appropriate replication (n=6 independent assays from two batches). The comparison with previous work (Wiseman et al., 2018) is appropriately cited and the improvement is substantial and well-documented.

results.result: Telacebec inhibits purified CIII2CIV2 with an IC50 of 53 ± 19 nM, which is in a similar range to concentrations needed to inhibit electron transfer in mycobacterial membranes and M. tuberculosis growth.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C94 and C5 are supported by experimental titration data (Figure 2C) with appropriate replication (n=3 independent titrations from two batches). The IC50 value is intermediate between membrane vesicle and bacterial growth assays, with reasonable speculative explanations provided for the differences (C95-C96).

results.result: The inhibitor-free structure shows endogenous MQ in the QP site at a position (Q1b) near the entrance, ~14-15 Å from the FeS cluster and His368, which is too far for rapid electron and proton transfer.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C106 are supported by cryoEM density data (Figure 3B) with quantitative distance measurements from the structural model. The inference that these distances are too far for rapid electron transfer (C106) is based on established biophysical principles and is appropriately qualified.

results.result: The structure of CIII2CIV2 with both DMWH2 and telacebec was determined at 3.0 Å resolution, revealing that telacebec binds deep within the QP site in a pose similar to UQ-analogue inhibitors in canonical CIII2.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C117 describe the successful structural determination of the telacebec-bound complex, supported by cryoEM data (Figure 3C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Table 1). The observation that telacebec requires substrate turnover for binding (C111-C112) is experimentally demonstrated, and the binding pose is clearly resolved in the structure.

results.result: Telacebec forms multiple interactions with CIII2CIV2 including a possible hydrogen bond between its N1 nitrogen and His368, hydrophobic interactions with Ile178, a possible halogen bond with Leu166, a possible hydrogen bond between Thr308 and the linker carbonyl, and aromatic-aromatic interaction with Phe156.
results.evaluation: Claims C118, C120-C124 describe specific protein-inhibitor interactions supported by structural data (Figure 3C-D) with quantitative distance measurements. While hydrogen bonds cannot be definitively confirmed at 3.0 Å resolution (appropriately noted), the positions are consistent with these interactions and the overall binding mode is well-supported.

results.result: The T313A mutation in M. tuberculosis (T308A in M. smegmatis) confers resistance to telacebec, likely by removing a stabilizing hydrogen bond with the inhibitor's linker region.
results.evaluation: Claims C130-C131 and C53 combine cited resistance data (Pethe et al., 2013) with structural interpretation from the current work (Figure 3C-D). The mechanistic explanation for resistance based on loss of the Thr308 hydrogen bond is a reasonable inference supported by the structural data.

results.result: The selectivity of telacebec for mycobacterial CIII2CIV2 may derive from the lack of Thr308 in mammalian CIII2 and potential steric clashes with mammalian residues Leu150 and Ile146.
results.evaluation: Claims C134-C135 are speculative inferences based on structural comparison (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D). While the structural differences are documented, the actual contribution of these differences to selectivity has not been experimentally validated. This would require testing telacebec against mammalian CIII2 or creating reciprocal mutations.

results.result: Telacebec binds only at the QP site and completely inhibits activity, indicating that MQ binding at other sites is not involved in electron transfer to oxygen.
results.evaluation: Claims C138-C139 are supported by the structural data showing telacebec binding exclusively at the QP site (Figure 3C) combined with the complete inhibition demonstrated in activity assays (Figure 2C). The inference that other MQ binding sites are not involved in catalysis is logical and well-supported.

results.result: The authors propose a model where MQH2 binds at a Q1b 'stand-by' position before moving to a Q1a position for oxidation, and that telacebec acts as a dual-site inhibitor blocking both positions.
results.evaluation: Claims C145-C151 and C6 present a mechanistic model combining structural observations with speculative inferences. While the structural data clearly show MQ at Q1b and telacebec occupying both Q1a and Q1b positions, the dynamic movement of MQH2 between these positions during catalysis (C146-C148) is speculative and not directly demonstrated. The model is reasonable but requires validation through additional experiments such as time-resolved studies or molecular dynamics simulations.

results.result: The structural analysis provides constraints for designing improved telacebec analogues with better pharmacokinetic and physicochemical properties, including analogues that avoid mycobacterial efflux pumps.
results.evaluation: Claims C126 and C128 are reasonable inferences from the detailed structural data showing protein-inhibitor interactions. The structure does provide a rational basis for structure-based drug design. The mention of efflux pumps (C128-C129) is appropriately cited to prior work (Jang et al., 2017).

results.result: Telacebec is one of only a few new drug classes in more than 50 years with demonstrated antituberculosis activity in humans, as shown by Phase 2 clinical trial data demonstrating decreased mycobacterial sputum load.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C51, and C152 are supported by appropriate citations to clinical trial data (de Jager et al., 2020) and provide important context for the significance of understanding telacebec's mechanism of action.
